7.4.1 Acknowledging Environmental, Social, and Governance Risks
Integrating environment, social, and governance (ESG) perspectives into BDC's risk management frame-
work, credit policies, and lending practices is one of our highest priorities. We aim to develop and fully align 
sustainability objectives with corporate strategy and risk appetite and integrating the key sustainability 
issues into our risk management practices. 
We understand that our lending portfolio bears environmental and social risks translated into credit risks, 
liability risks, as well as having direct impact on individuals and businesses. Concurrently, we are exposed to 
external E&S risks that need to be taken into consideration, as it could be translated into loss of security 
value and increased loss given default.
Accordingly, Banque du Caire is currently revamping the risk management framework to incorporate and 
consider all external and internal risks, including ESG risks. Appropriate management of ESG risks in lending 
portfolios should reduce potential future losses. BDC seeks to contribute to a positive societal impact while 
effectively managing risks and therefore maximizing returns.

Digitization
In accordance with our transformation journey, the digitalization framework will change day-to-day 
business, making it a more swift and efficient process. The microfinance unit will implement a digitalization 
project in 2020, in which all microloan submission and acquisition papers are to be submitted digitally. This 
will enable our loan process to become more convenient and reachable to clients in remote areas, who have 
no access to financial services. 
In line with our 5-year strategy, Banque du Caire is planning to expand its network of branches and open 
around 14 new branches in 2020, with the goal to reach a well distributed network of 308 branches in 2022. 
In addition to the financial soundness of opening a new branch, BDC considers primarily closing geographical 
gaps, and specifically targeting different market segments and customer categories to reach the unbanked. 
This is evident in our iconic Siwa branch established in 2014 which serves 1190 customers in an area where 
BDC is the only financial institution operating.

Mortgage Finance and Pensions
Not only does Banque du Caire focus on geographical proximity, but also, we provide affordable and low-cost 
financial products to meet the needs of underprivileged clients. In line with the CBE initiative, BDC offers 
mortgage finance catering to the low-income segment with very relaxed payment plans and an exemption 
from all fees and commission, reaching 26,077 clients with total bookings of EGP 486 MN as of 2019. It is 
important to note that the balance of the mortgage loan portfolio has reached EGP 2.1 billion in the year 
2019, compared to EGP 1.7 billion in the year 2018, with a growth rate of about 25 percent. Moreover, 
Banque du Caire offers pension loans to serve underprivileged customers with suitable loan amount and an 
easy installment plan that meets their needs.
Aman Certificate
In 2018, BDC issued Aman Certificate with the objective of engaging 
the unbanked and underprivileged in the formal banking sector. 
Targeting underprivileged Egyptians from the age of 18 to 59 years, 
and for low-income laborers/workers, this certificate of deposit is 
bundled with a life insurance policy in case of death or accident. This 
CD is offered both to individuals and enterprises’ Laborers/workers, 
with the number of clients reaching 23,219 individuals and 31,020 
enterprises, totaling' EGP 26,086,500 and EGP 32,929,500, 
respectively.

Meeza Card
Introduced by CBE as one of the financial inclusion 
initiatives that promote a cashless society, Meeza is the 
Egyptian national payment scheme that aims to 
facilitate the transition to a less cash-dependent 
economy. Launched in February 2019, BDC offers three 
types of Meeza Cards (Debit, prepaid, or payroll card).
The prepaid cards are issued based on simple Know 
Your Customer (KYC) requirements and are exempted 
from administrative fees for a limited period. Meeza 
allows customers to withdraw cash as well as recharge 
it through ATMs, as well as enabling them to conduct 
AMAN

purchases and e-commerce transactions on a local basis. Meeza Debit cards are issued with lower fees to 
encourage the unbanked to open new accounts in addition to prepaid cards for the youth and the payroll 
customers. The general objective of launching Meeza and similar initiatives is the sustained improvement of 
quality of life of the low-income rural population while at the same time seeking to assure an effective and 
efficient contribution by the rural economy to the national development process.

Qahera Cash Merchant Wallet
In October 2019, Banque du Caire launched its merchant wallet service using QR 
Code technology. The merchant wallets platform (UPG) provides a new digital 
payment acceptance method, which enables the merchants to receive their 
payment digitally and instantly from any mobile wallet in the market. The product 
spares both parties (merchant & consumer) the hassle of cash transactions and 
all related security and hygiene issues. The Merchant wallet service registration is 
of zero cost and requires no maintenance at all. The service also enables 
merchants to receive payments securely and instantly. It has a “request to pay” 
feature to support phones without cameras to perform the same transactions 
done by smartphones without scanning the QR code. BDC will continue the 
efforts exerted to partner with 34,000 merchants by the end of 2020 and 
100,000 by the end of 2021.

ed/located.

the SMEs' expansion strategy, with a goal of reaching 30 BCs by the end of 2020. Each business center is 
led by a team of experienced Relationship Managers (RMs) & Team Leaders providing exceptional services

The year 2019 witnessed significant achievements in terms of expanding Banque du Caire international 
presence. With an emphasis on Egypt's top trade partner countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Middle 
East, the Bank successfully increased its global network to 460 correspondents in 2019, up from 400 in 
2018. It also helped the Bank diversify its funding sources and increase its market share in Egyptian expatri-
ate remittances. It also strengthened business relations with a wide range of NBFIs in the local market, 
boosting the Bank's assets, liabilities, and revenues.

another achievement for Banque du Caire this year. The RO is geared towards increasing activities between

referrals.

ABOUT THE 
REPORT 
Scope of the Report
This report represents the first Integrated Sustainability report for Banque du Caire (BdC), and its fourth Sustainability 
Report in accordance to GRI. The report provides stakeholders with comprehensive information about the financial 
performance of the Bank and its sustainability-related activities.
Throughout the report, the terms “BdC” , “the Bank” , and “We” are used to refer to Banque du Caire.
Reporting Guidelines 
The report aligns with the IIRC Integrated Reporting Framework and is in accordance with the Sustainability Reporting 
Standards outlined by the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) for the year 2021 (GRI 2021).
It is aligned with UN SDGs and the national sustainable development strategy Egypt Vision 2030. It is also aligned with 
the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) ESG Index. Banque du Caire has also been a participant of the UN Global Compact since 
2016 and reports annually on the 10 principles. 
Reporting Period 
The information presented in this report reflects BdC activities for the calendar year 2022 (January 1-December 31, 
2022) and provides a comprehensive overview of the Bank's endeavors and achievements throughout this period. 
Additionally, it highlights any significant efforts conducted prior to or following this timeframe that hold relevance to the 
various sections of the report. The report will be updated annually to comply with Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) 
regulations. 
Forward-looking Statement

ABOUT 
BDC
Since its establishment in 1952, Banque du Caire (BdC) has positioned itself as one of Egypt's leading and expansive 
financial institutions. BdC is dedicated to offering a comprehensive array of banking services and products tailored to the 
individual needs of its massive and diverse customer base of more than 3 mn customers, including individual retail 
customers as well as large, medium, small, and micro-enterprises. Continuously expanding its network of branches and 
ATMs, the Bank guarantees accessibility and convenience for its clients. It operates currently through a network of 248 
branches and 1650 ATMs across the country. In the era of digital transformation, Banque du Caire continues to 
demonstrate its commitment to enhancing digital banking services, modernizing operational systems, and aligning with 
international governance standards. The Bank has witnessed significant uptake, with 1 mn customer subscribing to 
digital services. 
Awards
BdC has received prestigious accolades, including being recognized as:
• The top CSR Bank in Egypt by Global Economics Magazine, Global Business Magazine, International Finance Magazine, 
and Global Business Outlook Magazine.
• The top T rade Finance Bank in Egypt by Global Business Magazine and Global T rade Review Magazine.
• The top-ranked for the Structured Financing Deal in North Africa by EMEA Finance. 
• The top-ranked for both Local Currency Deal and Local Custodian by EMEA.

OUR COMMITMENT
TO SUSTAINABILITY
"Banque du Caire is an active player contributing to the creation of a socially inclusive, ecologically sustainable, and 
well-governed world. Since joining the United Nations Global Compact in 2015, sustainability has been an integral part 
of the Bank's business model, anchored in its Code of Conduct. BdC’s sustainability strategy centers around sustainable 
finance, policies, and commitments. The Bank adopted targets including team capacity building, sustainability reporting, 
and stakeholder engagement. The Bank has set ambitious targets, including aligning credit portfolios with the Paris 
Agreement, implementing an Environmental and Social Management System (ESMS), and promoting sustainability 
awareness. BdC integrates sustainability into its core operations through the Sustainability Steering Committee by 
addressing risks and opportunities and overseeing green initiatives. The Bank is a signatory of UNEP FI’s Principles for 
Responsible Banking and the UN Global Compact. In addition, BdC voluntarily commits to international standards such 
as the UN SDGs and Paris Agreement.

CHAIRMAN
MESSAGE
The year is 2022 and the world as we know is changing considering the current circumstances our world is 
going through. Socio-economic conditions and geo-political conflicts have dominated the news and to add to it, 
the world has been witnessing environmental crisis day after another. Fortunately, it is not too late for action, 
and at Banque du Caire (BdC), we are continuing on the path of sustainable transformation that will help 
guide us and the communities we serve through every challenge awaiting us. 
T owards the end of 2022, COP 27 rose as a beacon of hope to help create a light at the end of the 
proverbial tunnel, a call-to-action for change, speaking on behalf of every nation on every continent on 
this planet we call home. And in alignment with the National and International agendas, BdC has set the 
strategic direction for how we will make our impact, changing the world by changing how we do 
business, one step at a time. 
Our transformational efforts are built on the foundation of an interconnected approach to change, 
embedding the pillars of governance, reporting, strategy, capacity building and sustainable finance 
into a single unified framework that enhance our impact and ensure compatibility with our 
business goals. This methodical approach ensures our exceptional growth rates to continue on a

Our Stakeholder Mapping & Engagement
Banque du Caire recognizes the critical importance of engaging with its diverse stakeholders to promote a sustainable 
and inclusive future. In this section, we explore the multifaceted relationships that BdC maintains with its customers, 
shareholders, regulatory bodies, community, environment, suppliers, board of directors, and employees, aiming to 
transparently communicate our improvement in fostering meaningful connections with a broad spectrum of 
stakeholders. 
The relationship between BdC and its stakeholders is not just transactional, but it includes meaningful communication 
and understanding, which are fundamental elements for the success of the Bank. Engaging with this wide range of 
stakeholders is not a one-time effort but an ongoing process consisting of regular updates, feedback mechanisms, and 
various channels of communication to keep stakeholders informed and involved, as well as to understand their 
expectations in order to meet their needs and deliver high-quality financial services while complying with regulations 
and maintaining ethical standards. Moreover, engagement with stakeholders helps the Bank to identify and address 
issues before they escalate, demonstrating a sense of responsibility and risk management.

Mr. Tarek Fayed is the Chairman and CEO of BdC, with over 32 years of banking 
experience in various fields including banking supervision, risk management, as well 
as corporate and investment banking.
Mr. Fayed is currently a board member of the Egyptian Banking Institute, Social Fund 
for Mortgage Finance, Egyptian Stock Market, Union of Arab Banks, Credit Guarantee 
Company (CGC), Cairo Leasing Company (CLC), General Assembly Egyptian Holding 
Company for Aviation, and the Federation of Egyptian Chambers of Commerce.
Prior to his tenure with BdC, Mr. Fayed spent 10 years working for the CBE, having 
joined the Bank during the second wave of the banking sector reform program. He 
has overseen several departments under banking supervision including ongoing 
surveillance, licensing and macroprudential supervision. He successfully shifted the 
supervisory framework from a compliance to a risk-based approach and introduced 
new supervisory tools such as early warning and stress testing. He also participated 
in the introduction of a large range of prudential regulations including Basel 
Standards. Additionally, he established Egypt’s first financial stability report in 2016 
and was also part of the CBE negotiation team with the International Monetary Fund

Anti-Money Laundering (AML)
The Anti-Money Laundering (AML) department at BdC is tasked with the responsibility of safeguarding the Bank against 
the risks associated with money laundering and terrorist financing. The department's key functions include:
• Assessing and reviewing customer acceptance and account openings from a risk perspective.
• Monitoring transactions for suspicious activities.
• Conducting sanctions screening to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements.
• Approving high-risk accounts.
• Reviewing FATCA customers to ensure compliance with international tax regulations.
• Providing comprehensive training on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Financing of T errorism (AML/CFT) 
requirements for all Bank employees.
Procedures to Ensure Anti-Money Laundering Compliance
Banque du Caire adheres to robust AML/CFT policies and procedures developed in accordance with local regulatory 
guidelines and international laws. These procedures cover customer acceptance requirements, transaction monitoring, 
and sanctions screening.
Detection Mechanisms for Anti-Money Laundering Activities
BdC utilizes an automated transactions monitoring system (SAS) to detect suspicious behaviors and transactions 
related to money laundering and terrorist financing. This system is equipped with ML&FT scenarios to identify various 
patterns and typologies of illicit activities. Additionally, staff members receive comprehensive training to recognize and

report any suspicious activities through assigned channels. The Safe Watch Sanction screening system is employed to 
ensure compliance with sanctions regulations and to prevent transactions involving sanctioned entities or individuals.
Reporting Suspicious Transactions
Staff members are required to report any suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing to the AML/CFT sector 
via the SAS system or through email using the Suspicious T ransaction Report (STR) or Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) 
form. The AML/CFT sector conducts investigations, and based on the analysis and findings, decides whether to report 
the case to the Egyptian Combating Money Laundering Unit (EMLCU) via the "GO AML" automated system or to file the 
case internally.
Awareness Initiatives
BdC has undertaken various internal and external awareness initiatives concerning anti-money laundering and 
anti-corruption. Notable examples include the publication of an AML guide in 2023 and an Anti-Bribery and Corruption 
(ABC) policy in 2022. Additionally, regular internal and external training sessions are conducted based on an annual plan 
approved by the Board of Directors.

done fairly, as such:

heads, and subordinates) as well as external parties (clients, suppliers, and competitors).
• Among other areas of conflict of interest, personal benefits or advantages should not be obtained from any of the 
aforementioned parties in any way.
• Employees of Banque du Caire are prohibited from investing their money in stock exchanges, and they are only 
permitted to deal in securities in the operations of public subscription, buying, and selling, according to a specific set of 
controls defined in our policy.
• No party is allowed to exploit any information available on some of the Bank’s contributions that are not available to 
dealers in the market or to deal in shares of companies related to the Bank. Employees who possess such essential 
information that is not available to the public as a result of their work or while carrying out their duties and job 
responsibilities are prohibited from purchasing the shares of any company in their name, spouse, or minor children. It is 
also prohibited to disclose this information to persons outside the Bank, work for external entities, or have personal 
relationships with staff.

especially in strong FX generating sectors such as hospitality, restaurants, and textiles. This expansion was facilitated by

Women Empowerment 
T o empower women financially, the Bokra savings account was launched in 2019 especially for women. It provides 
them with interest as well as life insurance benefits. The duration and installments are determined by the client, starting 
from 1 year to 10 years and installments started from 100 EGP. The account also allows women to take credit facilities 
or credit card issuance with the same currency. 
Youth Empowerment 
In support of youth aged 16 years and above, BdC launched the T elda card in 2022, allowing youth to open an account 
and issue cards without a guardian, using only their national ID. They can also enjoy the receival of their payout on their 
accounts. T elda prepaid cards are another value offering, allowing youth to issue cards without opening an account. 
Parents can purchase up to five cards for themselves and their children, starting at 10 years old, and replenish the card 
with amounts to give children a sense of independence by using the card.

Transforming Our Supply Chain 
Consequent to the intricate and complicated nature of our industry, an ERP system is of great importance to our Bank. 
Strong management control is required, but we currently fulfill our financials and supply-chain management needs 
through a manual process or an outdated in-house solution. Hence, we have already begun the process of securing an 
ERP system to facilitate the flow of work and eliminate errors and issues that arise. We have completed all tender 
formalities and are currently waiting for the approval to start contracting with the vendor and launching the project. 
Expected results and impacts can be summarized in the ability to control all requests, have more visibility on our 
purchasing history, as well as a better secure procurement process. 
Economic Challenges 
The Egyptian pound has witnessed a devaluation of over 70% since March 2022. This devaluation has had a significant 
impact on the foreign exchange rate, causing it to fluctuate. At BdC, we have been facing a challenge in securing 
payments in USD as we must pay in Egyptian pounds, and we expect that the devaluation will be even more 
pronounced next year. We have been facing difficulties acquiring proposals from foreign suppliers, and we face the risk of 
being unable to commit to such proposals.

Advancing Environmental Stewardship (Natural Capital)  
BdC acknowledges the critical role it plays in the scope of climate change and environmental sustainability. We realize 
our responsibility to protect our environment and find means to reduce our carbon footprint.
 
In light of that, BdC has taken actions to optimize its use of resources through its fixed assets department, which 
launched the “Environmental Sustainability and Asset Management in Action” program targeting 2024. From 2020 to 
2021, the fixed assets team managed to finalize most of BdC’s physical inventory, decreasing the missing assets, 
monitoring the stolen assets, and disposing the non-needed and faulty assets. This action resulted in enabling us to 
track our owned assets, which in turn reduced unnecessary equipment purchases &costs.
A lot of benefits from asset management come through better energy efficiency. Through the initiative we can ensure 
that sustainability is aligned with the asset life-cycle analysis & Asset Disposal. In addition, we started adopting a green 
culture in which we reduce the current use of papers to request for asset replacement, movement and disposal. 
The Bank has created a comprehensive environmentally friendly branch in Siwa, employing materials that align with 
international standards for sustainability.

broad portfolio of tailored banking services, innovative digital solutions, and diverse non-

individuals, microenterprises, small and medium-sized businesses, and large institutions

The Bank’s regional presence extends beyond Egypt’s borders, with a representative office 
in the United Arab Emirates and a strategic subsidiary in Uganda-strengthening its role as 
a regional financial player and a stable gateway to cross-border banking services.
Guided by a vision toward sustainability, BdC continues to drive forward with strategic 
initiatives that integrate responsible banking practices, digital transformation, and inclusive 
finance. As it looks to the future, Banque du Caire remains steadfast in its mission: to 
empower clients, foster lasting partnerships, and support Egypt’s long-term economic 
prosperity.

2024 BdC  
Economic Performance
In 2024, BdC demonstrated robust financial progress, underscoring its resilience and 
strong economic stewardship. The Bank recorded a 56.2% increase in revenue, rising 
from EGP 22.2 Bn in 2023 to EGP 34.7 Bn in 2024, reflecting substantial growth in 
core banking activities and overall operational scale.
Profitability indicators strengthened significantly, with ROAE rising by 8% and ROAA 
improving by 0.95%, affirming more effective capital utilization and asset efficiency. 
The net interest margin increased by 1.59%, signaling higher returns from interest-
earning activities.
Operational efficiency also improved, as the cost-to-income ratio dropped by 5.06%, 
reflecting stronger income performance and cost control measures. BdC enhanced 
its liquidity position, with the gross loans to deposits ratio increasing by 5.02% and 
the net loans to deposits ratio rising by 4.43%, indicating better credit deployment. 
Asset quality saw marginal improvement, with NPLs-to-gross loans down 0.36%. 
The capital adequacy ratio remained solid, with only a slight decrease of 0.13%, well 
above regulatory thresholds.
Additionally, the Bank’s investment portfolio reached EGP 6.34 Bn, reinforcing its 
dedication to sustainable, diversified returns.

Generating Value  
Through the Six Capitals
BdC’s business strategy is fundamentally centered on sustainable value creation. Guided by 
a long-term vision and its profound awareness of stakeholder needs, the Bank integrates 
the six capitals (financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, and 
natural) into its strategic planning and execution. This integrated thinking ensures that value 
is not created in isolation, but through a balanced, responsible approach that enhances, 
preserves, or transforms these capitals over time.
The Bank’s strategic pillars intersect across the six capitals to create long-term sustainable 
value. One pillar may directly support more than one capital, while others provide indirect 
reinforcement. This integrated approach ensures that operational decisions contribute not

Our Targets
In alignment with our long-term sustainability vision, BdC has set forth a series of strategic targets 
aimed at embedding environmental, social, and governance considerations across all aspects of our 
operations. These targets reflect our proactive approach to managing sustainability-related risks and 
opportunities, while also reinforcing our dedication to responsible banking, regulatory alignment, and 
global sustainability frameworks. 
To further demonstrate our commitment to sustainability, the Bank has identified a comprehensive 
set of strategic targets:
• Align our credit portfolios with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the E&S policy, which 
includes a commitment to implement climate impact assessment tools, such as carbon intensity.
• Launch initiatives that reflect BdC’s commitment to being a responsible and sustainable bank.
• Implementation of an ESMS (environmental and social management system).
• Train all BdC staff on sustainability (general and multi-tiered educational approaches).
• Develop green/sustainability-linked products, either conventional or tailored.
• Continue to issue annual sustainability reports, including the UNGC CoP, GRI, PRB and carbon 
footprint reports.
• Embedding sustainability policies into our business model.
• Use PRB and carbon footprint recommendation reports to guide our strategic direction.
• Empower and educate clients by creating sustainability awareness campaigns.

ESG Highlights
Economic
• BdC recorded a 56.2% increase in revenue, rising from EGP 22.2 Bn in 2023 to EGP 34.7 Bn in 2024. 
• BdC delivered strong profitability indicators, including net interest margin increasing by 1.59% and 
cost-to-income ratio dropping by 5.06% in 2024. 
• BdC expanded its lending portfolio, with SME loans reaching EGP 26.8 Bn, marking a 12% annual 
growth and representing 8% of the Bank’s total loan portfolio.
• The Bank significantly strengthened physical and digital accessibility through a 7.8% expansion of 
the ATM network from 1,670 in 2023 to reach 1,800 machines in 2024, achieving 100% accessibility 
nationwide. 
Environment
• The Bank rolled out a dynamic e-statement feature, offering digital, accessible, and environmentally 
friendly alternatives to paper-based communication. 
• BdC offered a range of environmentally beneficial retail lending products in 2024, including solar 
power loans and electric car loans in support of Egypt’s low-carbon transition.
• BdC achieved a significant reduction in its overall water consumption, decreasing usage from 
528,817.75 m³ in 2023 to 329,056.03 m³ in 2024, representing a 37.78% decline.
Social 
• BdC reinforced financial inclusion by directing 24% of total retail lending to female clients, expanding 
youth outreach with a 53.4% rise in Waffar Savings Accounts from 36,580 in 2023 to 56,123 in 2024.
• BdC employed 207 people with disabilities in 2024, accounting for 2.4% of its workforce.

Material Matters
At Banque du Caire, we adopt the principle of double materiality as a cornerstone of our sustainability strategy and reporting process. 
As recognized by global standards such as the GRI, SASB, and emerging regulatory frameworks, this principle enables us to 
understand and respond to sustainability matters from two critical perspectives:
Materiality Assessment Process
In 2024, BdC further refined its materiality assessment process to enhance relevance, inclusivity, and 
alignment with international best practices. This process unfolds across three integrated phases:
             Strategic Alignment 
             and Framework Integration
We begin by anchoring our assessment in key frameworks that 
guide our disclosures and performance evaluations. These include:
•  Egypt’s national development priorities and Vision 2030,
•  The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),
•  Global standards such as the GRI Standards and SASB’s Commercial Banks guidelines
•  Evolving ESG disclosure requirements from regulatory authorities
This strategic alignment ensures that our material topics reflect both global 
sustainability priorities and national development needs.
              Evaluating 
              Material Impacts
Each potential material topic is assessed based on:
•  Its actual and potential impact on people, communities, and the planet, across 
    our operations and value chain (impact materiality)

BdC places a high priority on integrating ESG considerations into its risk management framework, credit 
policies, and lending practices. A core component of this integration is the environmental and social risk 
management (ESRM) framework, which encompasses an environmental and social (E&S) lending policy and 
associated procedures. These are designed to identify and manage E&S risks, monitor and report on them, 
and ensure that relevant staff are appropriately trained.
The ESRM framework is structured to meet applicable regulatory requirements and clearly defines the roles 
and responsibilities of all stakeholders involved in the credit process. Key actions under this framework 
include:
•  Initial E&S risk screening of lending proposals
•  Use of an exclusion list for prohibited activities
•  Classification of transactions based on risk categorization (low, medium, high)
•  Conducting environmental and social due diligence (ESDD)
•  Development and monitoring of an environmental and social action plan (ESAP)
To ensure effective implementation of the ESRM system, BdC has established a dedicated environmental 
and social risk department. This department is responsible for conducting E&S risk assessments for large 
corporate clients and supervising the MSME framework for the SME segment. It also plays a central role in 
categorizing the Bank’s portfolios based on E&S risk exposure.

Audit Independence
The internal audit function at BdC ensures its independence through a direct functional reporting line to the audit 
committee of the Board of Directors. Internal auditors strictly adhere to the internal audit code of conduct and are 
required to declare any potential or perceived conflicts of interest, thereby upholding objectivity and professional 
integrity.
Audit Framework 
BdC maintains a robust internal audit framework designed to keep audit practices effective and aligned with 
global best practices. The Bank reviews and updates its audit manual, charter, and audit plans on an annual basis-
or more frequently if needed. These updates are guided by the latest Global Internal Audit Standards issued by 
the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA), regulatory requirements from CBE, and key operational indicators such as 
fraud incidents, penalties, staff turnover, and major changes in the organizational structure.
The Bank conducts comprehensive risk assessments at least annually to identify and prioritize audit areas. These 
assessments include ESG risks. Risk evaluation considers inherent risk and the effectiveness of internal controls 
to determine residual risk, which shapes audit planning and resource allocation.

A.  Expanding Access: Strengthening ATM and POS Networks Across Egypt
At BdC, expanding access to financial services remains a central pillar of our dedication to inclusion and 
customer-centric growth. In 2024, we significantly strengthened our physical and digital touchpoints, 
growing our ATM network to 1,800 machines, up from 1,670 in 2023-a 7.8% increase.
This expansion is driven by a deliberate and data-informed approach. Each year, we design a detailed 
deployment strategy that targets underserved and high-potential areas. Prior to installation, the 
placement of every ATM undergoes a comprehensive feasibility assessment, considering key factors 
such as:
•  Population density and foot traffic
•  Concentration of BdC customers
•  ATM coverage by competitors
•  Brand visibility and strategic relevance
To further refine our network strategy, we collaborated in 2024 with ADHOC, a leading market research 
agency. Their nationwide survey enabled us to assess our competitive positioning and identify optimal 
ATM locations, enhancing service accessibility while boosting our market presence.

to elevate customer satisfaction, expand digital banking adoption, and deliver a truly inclusive banking 
experience. We remain committed to achieving 100% nationwide coverage, ensuring that individuals in

BdC governs its procurement activities with integrity and transparency, operating under a formal 
procurement policy and comprehensive supply chain procedures that guide supplier engagement. The

form of favoritism in dealings with suppliers. All employees are strictly prohibited from receiving personal 
benefits or privileges from suppliers and must avoid any manipulation or misuse of information acquired 
through their roles at the Bank. This policy ensures that all supplier relationships are based solely on 
merit and fairness.

are actively communicated to all suppliers to ensure their full awareness and adherence. During the 
reporting period, four confirmed incidents of corruption-related violations were identified, resulting in 
the termination or non-renewal of the respective supplier contracts.

            SME  
            Sectoral Distribution 
BdC supports a diverse range of economic sectors through its SME lending portfolio. In 2024, 
manufacturing remained the dominant sector in BdC’s SME portfolio, followed by trade and services. The 
agriculture and construction sectors also recorded growth, reflecting the ongoing diversification in the 
Bank’s SME portfolio.
            SME  
            Digital Transformation
The expansion of the internet and mobile banking has enabled clients to access a wide range of services 
remotely and securely. Clients can review account summaries and statements, transfer funds to BdC 
accounts, Meeza wallets, and prepaid cards, and conduct both domestic and cross-border transfers via 
ACH and SWIFT.
In addition, they can set up standing transactions, execute bulk payments to employees and suppliers, 
submit trade finance requests, and request bank drafts, custom certificates, and check books.
The adoption of digital services has also contributed to the growth of SME lending. Services such as 
online loan applications and the I-Sign digital signature solution enhance convenience by allowing clients 
to sign documents from their own premises, supporting time-efficient, cost-effective, and paperless 
banking. Moreover, the integration of automated credit scoring facilitates faster loan disbursement.

            SME  
            Non-Financial Services 
Each year, more than 30,000 clients benefit from BdC’s non-financial services, delivered through eight 
business development hubs operating under the CBE’s NilePreneurs initiative, which supports SMEs as 
part of the national financial inclusion agenda. These services target start-ups, entrepreneurs, and SMEs 
across Egypt’s governorates. 
BdC’s non-financial support includes facilitating access to finance, assistance with licenses, commercial 
registration, and activity registration. Additionally, the business development hubs focus on knowledge 
dissemination, covering areas such as financial planning, budgeting, interpretation of financial statements, 
and raising awareness of both bank and non-bank financing options. 
Furthermore, the hubs provide support in conducting feasibility studies, developing business models, 
and delivering training in financial analysis and project planning. The Bank also facilitates networking 
services, connecting SMEs with commercial chains, peers, and supply chains. This comprehensive 
support framework equips SMEs with tools, resources, and knowledge essential for sustainable growth 
and enhanced competitiveness.

BdC’s microfinance offering includes a diverse range of products tailored to meet the needs of underserved 
populations. These include buyout products, which support clients in refinancing or transferring existing 
loans from other institutions under more favorable terms. The Bank also provides asset-based financing, 
such as vehicle and motorcycle loans, enabling micro-entrepreneurs to acquire tools essential to their 
business operations. 
In line with its digital transformation strategy, BdC offers digital lending services that enhance 
accessibility and convenience for clients, particularly in remote or rural areas. Additionally, the Bank adopts 
a supportive approach to defaulters by offering practical solutions through the rescheduling policy. This 
approach helps clients overcome temporary financial difficulties and maintain continuity in their income-
generating activities. In 2024, the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio in the microfinance portfolio stood at

	 						Environmental	&	Social	Integration	
              in Corporate Lending Process 
BdC applies a structured Environmental and Social Risk Management (ESRM) framework alongside a 
dedicated Environmental and Social (E&S) lending policy to guide its corporate lending process. The Bank 
is actively enhancing its screening mechanisms to support effective E&S impact assessments, which 
inform lending decisions and help implement appropriate mitigation measures.
Clients are evaluated not only based on financial criteria-such as creditworthiness, liquidity, asset 
base, track record, and risk management practices-but also on environmental and social (E&S) risks. 
BdC categorises its lending portfolio based on sectoral and environmental classifications provided by 
the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA), the Industrial Development Authority (IDA), and the 
European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
When significant risks are identified, BdC collaborates with clients to develop Environmental and Social 
Action Plans (ESAPs), which outline specific mitigation measures and timelines to ensure compliance 
with Egyptian environmental regulations and applicable international standards.

D&SF and its Strategic Role
In alignment with BdC’s strategy to position itself as a fully integrated financial services provider, the 
Debt & Structured Finance (D&SF) division continued to strengthen its role as a key market player in 
2024. Established in 2018 during the Bank’s restructuring phase, the division offers specialized financing 
solutions, including syndicated loans, project finance, structured finance products, and debt capital 
market instruments, alongside financial advisory and agency services. This strategic focus has enabled 
BdC to capture larger and more complex transactions, expanding its market share and reinforcing its 
reputation for technical expertise. 
The division also played a significant role in the Debt Capital Market (DCM), acting as Placement Bank in 
seven issuances totaling EGP 9.8 Bn, while supporting Egypt’s sustainable development goals through 
innovative financing solutions such as the country’s first sustainability-linked Sukuk, contributing to 
financial inclusion and women empowerment.

Remittances
In 2024, BdC continued to deliver efficient and secure financial solutions to individuals and businesses, both domestically 
and across borders. These services remain fundamental to enhancing economic connectivity and facilitating trade 
flows. 
BdC provides access to remittance services through an extensive global network of exchange companies and foreign 
banking partners. This network enables customers abroad to send funds directly to BdC accounts or other banks in 
Egypt. In 2024, a total of 988,917 clients relied on BdC’s remittance services, representing 24% of our total client base. 
The total value of remittances processed through the Bank in 2024 reached EGP 2,356.6 Bn, a 43% increase compared 
to the previous year. This growth was driven by several measures implemented during the year. The onboarding of 
new exchange companies and aggregators significantly expanded our international remittance network, improving 
accessibility for customers abroad. Furthermore, reductions in correspondent banking fees made transfers more cost-
effective, encouraging higher volumes of remittances. The Bank also witnessed notable improvements in its digital 
channels and streamlined processes.

           BdC’s Inclusion 
           and Clientele Growth
Youth-Focused Banking Solutions
BdC actively promotes youth financial inclusion by enabling early and independent access to banking 
services. The Waffar Savings Account allows individuals aged 15 and above to open accounts without 
the need for a guardian, empowering young people to begin managing their finances at an early 
stage. To further extend accessibility, the Bank offers the Telda Prepaid Card, which offers fully digital 
onboarding through agent banking, helping to bridge the gap between young customers and formal 
financial services.
Women’s Financial Empowerment
BdC supports women’s financial inclusion by offering tailored financial products and focused outreach. 
A key initiative is the Baseeta Project, offered in collaboration with Coptic Orphans, which provides 
savings accounts for single and widowed mothers who are recipients of charitable donations. This 
initiative aims to enhance financial independence and promote long-term financial security for women, 
especially those from marginalized backgrounds.

• VRV HVAC systems: The installation of variable refrigerant volume systems offers enhanced energy efficiency 
and personalized climate control.
• Temperature regulation: To comply with the Central Bank of Egypt’s environmental guidance, all air 
conditioning units are set to 25°C to conserve energy without compromising comfort.
• Motion sensor lighting: Motion-activated lighting systems are being installed in the Bank’s new administrative 
capital building to reduce unnecessary electricity usage in low-occupancy areas.
• LED lighting systems: All renovated branches now utilize energy-efficient LED lighting, significantly reducing 
electricity consumption and carbon emissions.
• Double flushing systems: In line with our water conservation strategy, we are deploying dual flushing 
systems across all branches-with 75% of installations already completed-to improve water efficiency and 
reduce overall utility demand.
Our environmental strategy is grounded in continuous improvement. As we move forward, BdC remains 
committed to advancing sustainable infrastructure upgrades, enhancing its operational footprint, and supporting

Development Goals.

in health, education, economic empowerment, environmental sustainability, and community development. In

Since its founding in 1952, Banque du Caire (BdC) has established itself as one of Egypt’s most prominent financial 
organizations. With over 3 million clients, BdC is committed to providing a wide range of banking services and products 
customized to meet each one’s specific needs—whether of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises or individual retail 
customers. The Bank continually grows the number of its branches and ATMs to ensure it is easily accessible to its

- Conciseness: BdC is committed to providing information that is clear and concise.

BDC Sustainability / Report 2023 
Material
Matters
The principle of double materiality, as recognized by the GRI and other leading standards, is a pivotal and integral part of 
sustainability reporting and strategic implementation. It requires an evaluation of materiality from two interconnected 
dimensions:
Financial Materiality: 
ESG and climate-related factors that could inﬂuence Banque du Caire’s ﬁnancial performance, risk proﬁle, and long-term 
sustainability (outside-in perspective).
Impact Materiality:
The eﬀects of the Bank’s business activities, including services and operations, on the environment and society (inside-out 
perspective).
Identifying Material Issues:
The Bank employs a thorough assessment to identify key issues, considering both positive and negative impacts. This 
methodology ensures that our sustainability eﬀorts align with broader societal and environmental goals while remaining 
integral to the success of the Bank's business model. Material topics are prioritized through an internal and external 
analysis in three key phases:
▪ Aligning with Strategic and Regulatory Frameworks:
The Bank incorporates its strategic priorities, SDGs, Egypt's national objectives, and regulatory mandates. It relies on 
established ESG standards and frameworks, such as GRI and the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) for 
Commercial Banks, to guide its disclosures and materiality assessments.
▪ Evaluating Material Impacts:

▪ Evaluating Material Impacts:
For each material topic, we assess the actual and potential direct impacts—both positive and negative—arising from our 
operations (impact materiality). Additionally, we evaluate the eﬀects on the Bank's ﬁnancial performance and positioning 
over the short, medium, and long term (ﬁnancial materiality). This assessment, shaped by risk management principles, 
considers the interests of key stakeholders and supports the Bank's ongoing success.
• Embedding Material Topics:
The identiﬁed material topics are integrated into the Bank’s sustainability agenda, serving as a focus for the upcoming year 
and future objectives.

The main risk categories and associated subcategories to which the Bank’s activities and business ventures may be exposed are included in the Bank’s Risk Registry, which provides 
the foundation for the Bank’s creation of risk management procedures and strategies and enables consistent risk identification. The primary risk categories for the Bank are: 
Credit Risk: Credit risk is a financial loss arising from a counterparty’s inability or unwillingness to meet an obligation; it constitutes the most significant risk a financial institution can 
face. One form of this risk is direct credit risk (default of on-balance-sheet credit exposure), while another is contingent credit risk (default off-balance-sheet credit exposure). 
Due to the materiality of credit risk, the Bank established an appropriate credit risk mitigation action environment. It implements a robust measurement and monitoring process as a 
means of ensuring adequate control over credit risk.  The Bank’s credit risk management function is primarily responsible for measuring, monitoring, managing, and limiting risks 
associated with credit across various lines of business, including corporations, SMEs, financial institutions, non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), retail, and microfinance. The 
parameters and methodologies utilized by the Bank to assess the materiality level of credit risk are highly dependent on the type of asset and its associated risk management and

Implementing a well-structured credit rating framework is crucial for effective risk management, and this can be achieved through the utilization of the Obligor Risk Rating (ORR) 
system. The ORR system assigns credit ratings to borrowers through a comprehensive evaluation process, which includes a stringent and consistent assessment of credit risk. This 
process accurately reflects a borrower’s creditworthiness and probability of default by analyzing financial indicators, qualitative assessments, and macroeconomic factors. The 
standards set by the Basel Committee ensure that this risk rating system includes regular reviews of clients’ creditworthiness, especially those with credit facilities. To further mitigate 
risk and prevent defaults, an Early Warning Signals (EWS) system should be implemented. 
EWS leverages various financial and non-financial performance indicators to identify potential issues early on, allowing for corrective actions before a client’s situation becomes 
irretrievable. This system spans multiple industries, enabling tailored responses to specific cases and ensuring proactive management of credit risks.
Retail Risk: This type of credit risk occurs in retail and microfinance portfolios. Accordingly, the Bank maintains a second line of defense in its retail risk function that is in charge of 
monitoring, quantifying, controlling, and restricting this risk.

Market Risk: A leading risk that the Bank faces is market risk, which encompasses potential losses resulting from unfavorable movements in market prices, which may negatively 
affect the value of the Bank’s investment positions for trading purposes. Examples of market risk include interest rate fluctuations, currency and exchange rate volatility, and invest-
ment uncertainties. Thus, various mitigation and prevention measures are employed to effectively address market-associated risks. 
For example, each day, the Treasury Middle Office (TMO) meticulously monitors and controls the Treasury group’s positions. These efforts involve overseeing the profit and loss (P&L) 
of treasury products, all executed transactions, mark-to-market (MTM) revaluation, foreign exchange (FX) prices, CBE reserve ratios, and fund transfer pricing (FTP). The TMO ensures 
that all these activities comply with the latest policy updates and regulatory requirements set forth by both BdC and the CBE, thereby maintaining robust risk management and 
regulatory adherence.
Liquidity Risk: The primary aim of the liquidity risk function is to assess, quantify, monitor, and manage this risk across the Bank. More broadly, to ensure it meets all payment 
obligations and holds sufficient cash and high-quality liquid assets, especially during periods of stress, the Bank strives to maintain adequate funding in terms of amount and duration.

In addition to ensuring that our employees act with integrity and honesty, BdC prioritizes our compliance with Egyptian 
laws and regulations and our dedication to the ethical, professional, and legal standards of our business. 
In this regard, we empower our employees with various communication channels, bolstering their conﬁdence and enabling 
them to raise any concerns about suspected illegal or unethical acts without fear of retaliation. These channels include a 
dedicated direct complaint number for BdC, an assigned email for whistleblowing, and handwritten letters. 
We have a standardized form for reporting illegal practices that is overseen by the Head of Business Ethics and approved 
by the Head of Compliance and Corporate Governance. When a concern is raised through any communication channel, 
employees are required to complete this form to initiate an investigation. The completed form is then shared with the heads 
of the relevant departments, including Inspections (audits), Legal Aﬀairs, Human Resources, and the Security Group. These 
departments prioritize the concern and thoroughly evaluate its validity. If the complaint is substantiated, we recommend 
appropriate remedial, disciplinary, or preventive actions. We will not tolerate any form of harassment or discrimination, 
whether by or against employees, clients, or anyone conducting or seeking business with our Bank. If an issue arises, we

is the responsibility of the Head of General Management.

Our Anti-Money Laundering (AML) department is responsible for safeguarding BdC against money laundering (ML) and 
terrorist ﬁnancing (TF)-related risks. Their responsibilities are:
▪ Working as the second line of defense and monitoring the controls of the businesses. 
▪ Executing sanction screening of customers against local and international lists.
▪ Analyzing and reviewing customer acceptance and account openings from a risk perspective.
▪ Tracking transactions for suspicious activities. 
▪ Monitoring Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) customers to ensure compliance with international tax 
regulations.
▪ Providing our employees with AML and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (CFT) requirements to ensure their awareness 
and understanding of related procedures. 
▪ Prompting updates to implement changes in regulations reﬂecting AML policies, procedures, and controls.
▪ Developing and implementing quality assurance testing to assess the eﬀectiveness of the AML/CFT program’s 
implementation and execution. 
We ensure AML compliance by adhering to solid AML/CFT policies and procedures. These procedures and policies are 
developed following local regulatory laws, best practices and guidelines. In addition to encompassing customer 
requirements, sanctions screening, and transaction oversight.

Reporting Channels for Suspicious Activities 
In the event of suspicious activity, staﬀ members are required to report such activity to the AML/CFT sector via the SAS 
system or by email using the Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) or Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) form. The cases 
then undergo investigations and analyses by the AML/CFT to decide whether to report the identiﬁed case to the Egyptian 
Combating Money Laundering Unit (EMLCU) through the “GO AML” automated system or ﬁle the case internally.

BdC has demonstrated substantial growth in operating revenue, reﬂecting the Bank’s ability to capitalize 
on market opportunities and enhance operational eﬃciency. Beginning with an operating revenue of EGP 
9,977 Mn in 2019, our operating revenue soared to EGP 22,224 Mn, reﬂecting a remarkable 122.8% 
increase in 2023. This consistent and robust growth trend indicates the Bank’s strong market position 
and commitment to maintaining sustainable ﬁnancial performance.
Reﬂecting our commitments to ﬁnancial stability and risk management, BdC has maintained a strong 
and improving capital adequacy ratio over the past ﬁve years. In 2019, our capital adequacy ratio stood 
at 15.83%, providing a solid foundation for the Bank’s operations. By 2023, this ratio had increased to 
17.35%, representing a signiﬁcant improvement. This increase demonstrates our prudent approach to 
capital management, ensuring that the Bank remains well-capitalized and capable of withstanding 
potential ﬁnancial shocks. The higher capital adequacy ratio also positions us favorably for future 
growth, enabling us to continue supporting our clients and investing in sustainable initiatives while 
maintaining a robust ﬁnancial buﬀer.

BdC is a leading ﬁnancial institution in Egypt, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). We are 
renowned for our steadfast commitment to promoting ﬁnancial inclusion throughout the country, in line with Egypt’s Vision 
2030 goals. BdC is dedicated to helping SMEs achieve their full potential and recognizing their vital role in the national 
economic growth. The Bank is devoted to providing exceptional services to enhance and continually improve, automate, 
and digitize SME products and services to enable clients to manage their daily transactions seamlessly. We aim to be the 
primary partner for SMEs' growth by supporting entrepreneurship. To achieve this, we integrate non-ﬁnancial services with 
our ﬁnancial solutions.
BdC SME group adopts a decentralized approach to engage with clients through a wide network of 53 dedicated SME 
business centers. utilizing on the Bank’s expanding network of 249 branches across Egypt’s governorates. Additionally, 
under the umbrella of Nile Preneurs initiative which is supported by the CBE in collaboration with Nile University, BdC has 
established 8 Business Development Services (BDS) Hubs and units dedicated to serving all clients by providing 
non-ﬁnancial services and consultations.

growth from 2022 to 2023, particularly in sectors like trade, which saw a growth of 127%; manufacturing, which saw a growth of 27%; and services, which saw

Furthermore, the Bank promoted a decentralization approach, achieving remarkable growth in both the number of clients and the total loan growth rate throughout

BDC Sustainability / Report 2023 
BdC acknowledges its crucial role as one of Egypt’s leading public banks in expanding all people’s access to ﬁnance. 
Promoting ﬁnancial inclusion and advancing digital transformation are key priorities in our strategy, aligning with the CBE’s 
laws and regulations, the strategic goals of Egypt’s Vision 2030, and the UN’s SDGs. In this regard, in July 2020, BdC 
submitted its ﬁnancial inclusion strategy, which will be in eﬀect until 2023.
At BdC, our ﬁnancial inclusion strategy ensures that individuals and businesses can access useful, aﬀordable ﬁnancial 
products and services that cater to their needs. This strategy encompasses transactions, payments, savings, credit, and 
insurance, all of which are delivered responsibly and sustainably. Furthermore, it strives to incorporate all underserved and 
underprivileged segments of society into the formal banking system by oﬀering solutions through our diverse products 
and services. In line with this strategy, we design speciﬁc products for women, youth, the elderly, people with disabilities, 
and other underprivileged and underserved groups. 
BdC Financial Inclusion Strategy Targets 
▪ Women: Clients who are working women, housewives, or own or seek to own private businesses 
▪ Youth: Clients from 16 to 35 years old.
▪ Unbanked: Clients new to the Bank and without an account at BdC.

To empower women ﬁnancially, BdC introduced a special savings product, the Bokra Account, in December 2019. This 
savings account, available in EGP and tailored for women, is designed for women to meet their future ﬁnancial needs. It 
provides life insurance and allows customers to make ﬁxed monthly installments over varying rates and gain their principal

In 2023, BdC expanded its reach to more unbanked individuals who owned prepaid cards. The features of the prepaid 
card for the unbanked are as follows:
Cards are issued to individuals above 16 years old.
▪ Parents can purchase up to ﬁve cards for themselves and their children (10 years old and up) and replenish the card 
with amounts to give children a sense of independence by using the card.
▪ Opening an account at BdC does not require the card to be issued.
▪ Customers can ﬂexibly replenish the card through any of the Bank branches or BdC ATMs that accept deposits.
▪ Cards can be used domestically and internationally for purchases and ATM withdrawals.
▪ Cards can be used for Internet purchases.

BdC has initiated a process to record information about customers with disabilities in the core banking system to better 
understand their needs based on their disabilities. Current measures implemented to meet the needs of blind or visually 
impaired customers, for example, include the provision of product and service applications in Braille, while Deaf or 
hard-of-hearing customers can access sign language materials for ﬁnancial inclusion products on CDs and our website. 
The Bank also oﬀers tailored incentives for customers with disabilities during the annual Financial Inclusion Special 
Needs Event, held from December 1 to 15; in 2023, we provided all our loan products with a 50% discount on

BdC leverages technology to expand access to our banking services, and digital capabilities are instrumental in this eﬀort. 
The Bank provides a range of innovative, user-friendly digital platforms and tools that cater to diverse customer needs, 
including those of underserved and unbanked populations. These initiatives include mobile banking apps, online account 
management, and digital payment solutions that streamline transactions and improve accessibility. By integrating features 
like account management through smartphones, digital wallets, and online support services, BdC ensures that customers 
can perform ﬁnancial activities conveniently and securely. These digital advancements are crucial in reaching individuals in 
remote or underserved areas and oﬀering them the opportunity to participate fully in the ﬁnancial system. To this end and 
considering the CBE’s national strategy, the Bank acted to enhance its digital capabilities - including how they are 
provided—to achieve ﬁnancial inclusion via the following measures: 
▪ Our partnership with Etisalat Misr enables Etisalat Misr customers to transfer, receive, and save money securely via the Etisalat 
Cash application.
▪ Instapay is a mobile application that enables clients to process electronic fund transfers instantly, seamlessly, and at any time.

75%. Furthermore, we are in the process of using lighting motion sensors to save energy in the new capital building.

establishing new hospitals, and ﬁnally, supporting governmental initiatives related to the health sector. 
In 2023, BdC allocated 39.2% of its CSR budget to the health sector activities.
Throughout 2023, BdC contributed toward supporting Magdi Yacoub’s Hospital for Cardiology, Ahl Masr Hospital, 57357 
Hospital, Red Crescent Hospital, El Nas Hospital and Ain Shams University Hospital. Through this support, these 
institutions were able to build new campuses, cover operational costs and purchase new state-of-the art equipment. The 
Bank also funded treatment with the Orman Association and participated in treating cases at Mansoura University Hospital.
As part of the extended eﬀorts to battle cancer and raise public awareness on the ﬁght against breast cancer, the Bank 
collaborated with Baheya Hospital and Baheya Foundation. Throughout this important partnership, the Bank has launched 
a new volunteering program for staﬀ, aiming to conduct regular visits to the hospital to provide emotional support to 
patients and assure them they are not alone in their ﬁght. This has been bolstered by the Bank’s extended donations to 
Cairo University Kasr El Ainy Hospital in support of its cancer facilities.

At BdC, our goal is to acquire the products and services we require while keeping our Bank’s moral principles and strategic goals in mind. We aim to meet our Bank needs with the best possible quality, 
the most competitive prices, and the quickest lead times. Throughout our supply chain, BdC collaborates with more than 575 vendors, consultants, and service providers from its network in 2023. The 
Bank has prepared a Procurement Policy and Supply Chain Procedures to manage our connection with our supply chain in a transparent and eﬀective manner. These documents seek to provide workers 
with guidance on how to engage with suppliers and to clarify the process.
Approximately 70% of our procurement budget is devoted to local vendors, and our procurement network comprises suppliers from throughout Egypt. To guarantee a network of integrity, we check our 
supply chain network for any infractions connected to corruption. Contract terminations with business partners have not occurred as a result of any infractions. Future plans call for the implementation of 
socially and ethically responsible supplier screening. 
In 2023, due to eﬀective procurement processes, costs were managed well, with a cost avoidance of EGP 13 Mn and savings of EGP 100 Mn.

This report is not only a great reflection of what we all faced this year and the series of challenges we faced head on, but also the solutions 
we came up with to combat these challenges and ensure our continuous success with minimal disturbance and optimum efficiency.

Responsible for managing, measuring, and monitoring all 
positions exposed to market risks and ensuring that the 
necessary limits are set to reduce and limit those risks 
related to the activities of the Treasury Group, money 
market, investment sector, and securities such as interest 
rates risk, currency and exchange rates risk, volatility risk, 
and investment risk. 
Treasury Middle Office
Monitors and controls the entirety of the Treasury Group’s 
positions on a daily basis including prices, and CBE 
reserve ratios to ensure that BdC is in line with the CBE’s 
updated policy changes and regulatory requirements.
Liquidity Risk
The liquidity risk function’s primary objective is to provide 
assessment, measurement, monitoring, and control of 
liquidity risk across the Bank. At an aggregate level, its goal 
is to maintain sufficient funding in amount and tenor to 
ensure all payment obligations and provide an appropriate 
amount of cash and high-quality liquid assets, even in 
times of stress.

Banking Book (IRRBB)
The primary responsibility of the IRRBB function is to 
monitor, assess, and control potential interest rate risks 
that arise from adverse market movements, it is imperative 
to accurately monitor the associated interest rate risk due 
to its material impact on our financial position.

Operational Risk
Following a comprehensive approach to operational risk 
management due to the inherent nature of operational risk 
within the Bank’s functions. The Bank’s approach aims at 
identifying and preventing fraudulent acts, business 
interruptions, cybersecurity attacks, non-conformant 
employee behavior, non-compliance with applicable laws 
and regulations, or failure of vendors to perform per their 
agreements. Events such as these have a direct impact on 
our operations and ability to deliver products and services 
to our stakeholders. The Department develops a structured 
risk and control self-assessment process to avoid financial 
losses, litigation, and regulatory fines, and other material 
damages.
Outsource Risk (Third-Party)
Outsource or third-party risk is the risk associated with 
transactions that occur through our third-party vendors. 
We monitor the relationships with all third-party vendors to 
ensure the continued sustainability of the business and to 
avoid any negative impact on business performance. We 
have developed a comprehensive third-party management 
program to ensure clear reporting and accountability 
chains, appropriate classification and optimization of 
vendor portfolios, managing transitions among third-party 
vendors, and monitoring the relationship between the Bank 
and these vendors.

Financial Institutions Division is a dynamic platform responsible for 
regulating Correspondent Banks, Non-Banking Financial Institutions, 
Financial Institutions Structured Products Division, and Remittances. 
To regulate our sustainable activities, our Financial Institutions Sector 
contains four main departments with various mandates as follows:
Financial 
Institutions 
● Correspondent Banking: positions BdC's business propositions across the globe through partnerships with over 600 banks across six 
continents.
● Non-Banking Financial Institutions: manages BdC's business relations with 170+, insurance companies, microfinance providers, securities 
brokerages, auto finance, factoring, leasing, funds, mortgage, and e-payment companies.
● Financial Institutions Structured Products Division: acts as a focal point in availing funding channels to BdC in partnership with DFIs & 
Multilateral Funds by conducting direct and indirect lending syndicated/bilateral loans. FISP serves in sustaining BdC’s presence in the global 
market, in addition to offering tailored solutions to better serve our clients’ business needs. Moreover, it manages BdC’s relationship with the 
international rating agencies.
● Remittances: plays a vital role in managing the Bank’s relationships with 70+ money transfer organizations worldwide to attract Egyptian 
expatriates’ remittances, a cornerstone of the Egyptian economy.

Types of Accounts
at BdC
01
Current Accounts
Manages client finances through Banque du Caire’s Current Account with on-demand access 
designed with a range of benefits to suit client’s banking needs.
02
Savings Accounts
Banque du Caire’s Savings Account offers a competitive periodic return which is calculated on a 
tiered-rate basis (monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, or annually). With flexibility of account 
withdrawal and deposit at any time.
03
Certificate of Deposits
Is a savings account that holds a fixed amount of money for a fixed period of time, such as six 
months, one year, or five years, and in exchange for interest. Clients can redeem their CDs, and 
receive the money originally invested plus any interest.
04
Time Deposits 
A deposit with a specific maturity date or a period to maturity, commonly referred to as its 
“term”. Time deposits differ from call deposits, such as savings or checking accounts, which can 
be withdrawn at any time, without any notice or penalty.

The main objective in liabilities portfolio growth during 2020 was to align with our strategy to increase our liabilities portfolio. 
Although the impact of COVID-19 challenged our liabilities portfolio growth from several perspectives, such as CBE decisions in 
decreasing the corridor rates and competitor’s movements in increasing some of their products interest rates. 
Accordingly, we took the 
following steps, 
● BdC Retail Liabilities diversiﬁed its pricing strategy 
across its wide range of products focusing on increasing 
its interest rates on Certiﬁcate of Deposits that reached up 
to 12.25%. This was done to cope with the ﬁerce 
competition in the market and sustain clients who needed 
long-term investment during the pandemic.
● BdC Retail Liabilities launched new products with a 
unique selling proposition to fulﬁll customer's savings and 
investment needs which contributed to acquiring fresh 
funds as well as New to Bank clients such as:
 ●  New Savings Account with daily interest rate.
 ●  Revamping the pension current account to 
    serve pensioners' needs.
● BdC Retail Liabilities launched a contest for all branches 
with EGP 6.2Bn, of which EGP 4.7Bn were from individual 
deposits, and EGP 1.5Bn from local business deposits.

Microﬁnance is a critical component to promoting and enhancing inclusion. In line with our aim to provide fair opportunities for 
all, our microﬁnance segment is an eﬀective tool for generating a positive impact on people and society. Led by a strong and 
experienced team, our Microﬁnance Department ensures the ease and speed of product procedures, diversiﬁcation of available 
products, high ﬁnancial capacity, and availability of liquidity necessary for ﬁnancing operations. With a geographical spread all 
over Egypt, BdC maintains the largest market share. 
Banque du Caire’s ﬁrst microﬁnance strategy was launched in 2001. The strategy aims to provide digital ﬁnancial services to 
micro-entrepreneurs at their workplace throughout the country. Through the experience we have in microﬁnance, which extends 
to over 20 years, we have provided about 1,300 million job opportunities and a sustainable production project that serves 
various segments, most notably the youth and female. 
Our distinction in this ﬁeld is due to our geographical spread, especially in the governorates of Upper Egypt, which represent 
53% of our total microﬁnance portfolio. Women represent 35% and youth 40% of the total number of clients.

We have numerous sectors receiving microﬁnance, 
including, commercial, services, industry, transport, and 
the professional sector. In 2020, we experienced a 
decreased growth rate due to a large number of customer 
activities being negatively impacted as a result of the 
COVID-19 pandemic. Further impacting our business, we 
were forced to utilize conservative policies that resulted in 
a cease of new loan issuing for about 9 months and 
postponing installments for 3 months which had a signiﬁ-
cant negative impact on the freedom of movement. 
Despite these challenges, we look forward to making 
breakthroughs in 2021 and creating lasting and enduring 
impact. 
Microﬁnance enterprise is deﬁned as the enterprise whose capital doesn’t exceed 50k EGP and its proﬁt or revenue doesn’t 
exceed 1Mn EGP, according to the CBE. We recognize that supporting micro-enterprises is one of the key components to 
maintaining and enhancing sustainable ﬁnance. We aim to provide products and services that best serve the interests of 
micro-enterprises to strengthen their institutional capacities and stimulate innovation. We support micro-enterprises through a 
range of innovative oﬀerings. Our creditworthiness assessment and underwriting process are characterized by their speed and 
ease. Our Time to Yes and Time to Cash, takes one day to approve or reject the case and to appear in the customer account.

Despite the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic and its profound impact on the economy and society, in 2020, CBU 
ambitiously maintained its transformation journey. CBU recognizes the importance of implementing quality management 
systems and has in turn developed new management systems to inculcate inclusion, maintain innovation, and facilitate 
economic prosperity while ensuring development and coordination on all fronts. 
Uninterrupted by COVID-19, the Product Development Unit was launched aiming to coordinate the development of all new 
products, track their performance, report to Executive Management on their viability, and monitor the performance of existing 
products. Moreover, 2020 witnessed the introduction and implementation of the Marketing Department responsible for 
enhancing the Bank’s brand positioning, aligning its eﬀorts with its core business strategy, and playing a key role in driving 
utilization, transaction volumes, and changing market perception of the Bank. 
To supplement these achievements and further measure and monitor progress, the Bank introduced several performance 
dashboards and reports to track performance against budget. Alongside that, to ensure responsible and strategic allocation of 
resources, CBU introduced capital planning and Eﬃcient Cost and Capital management. 
The Bank experienced a reduction in cost to income ratio from 133% to 100% with a loss of UGS 2.8Bn less than the budgeted 
loss of UGX 5.6Bn.

CLC is BdC’s leasing arm that was established in March 2018 as an Egyptian Joint Stock Leasing Company under the provision 
of law No. 159 for the year 1981 with an Authorized Capital of EGP 500Mn. It was established to provide leasing products and 
services to meet corporate and SME capital expenditure needs for a wide variety of assets covering all industries. Although it is 
a newly established company, CLC is a proﬁtable investment as it successfully broke even during its ﬁrst year of operations, 
realizing an impressive ROE of 15%.
As part of our strategy to expand product oﬀerings to include non-banking ﬁnancial products, aiming at promoting ﬁnancial

Driving 
Financial 
Inclusion
Financial inclusion means that individuals and businesses have access to useful and aﬀordable ﬁnancial products and services 
that meet their needs – transactions, payments, savings, credit, and insurance – delivered responsibly and sustainably. At BdC, 
we ensure that we integrate all underserved and underprivileged segments in society into the formal banking system and 
provide them with solutions, through our various and diversiﬁed products and services. We cater speciﬁc products to women, 
youth, the elderly, and other underserved segments in society. We also ensure that people with disabilities are well served 
through our specially crafted products and services. We comply with all CBE laws and regulations regarding ﬁnancial inclusion 
and ﬁnancial literacy and ensure that our internal strategy is aligned with the CBE’s strategy, Egypt Vision 2030, and UN SDGs 
to ensure that no one is left behind.

Remittances
Remittance has a positive impact on serving a wide segment of Egyptians working abroad; as it provides them with a quick and 
safe way to send money to their families.
We already had a role in developing this service by serving The Egyptian expats resident in Jordan, sending our representative to 
market incoming money transfers from Jordan to Egypt, as well as opening accounts for Egyptian expats residents in Jordan.
We are planning to develop remittance to be a more eﬃcient tool for ﬁnancial inclusion using digital channels to serve families to 
send and receive their savings without visiting branches, which will help our customers in rural areas. 
We plan to launch Prepaid Remittance Card - a branded MasterCard - for customers receiving remittances from abroad in 
Egyptian Pounds and who do not have bank accounts.

Mobile Cash Withdrawal (MCW) solution is an innovative system enabling BdC to provide our customers with a cash withdrawal 
service initiated from a mobile device and fulﬁlled via ATMs. It complements the existing functionality of ATMs by providing 
quicker and more convenient access to cash than existing card-based systems, in addition to providing potentially increased 
transaction security.
Digital lending oﬀers us a lot of opportunities to improve productivity, close more loans and increase revenue per loan with 
cheaper and faster automated services.

Battling COVID-19
With its devastating effects on health and businesses globally, the COVID-19 crisis transformed the way we live and operate. It 
presented many new challenges to our operations, forcing us to reassess existing policies and strategies. Due to its impact on 
our operations, retail banking and direct sales were the most affected departments due to 3% corridor cuts and CBE regulations 
to postpone lending installments for 6 months. As a result, our call centers were inundated with calls received from customers to 
inquire about the CBE initiatives. 
In the face of all challenges, we actively apply all health and safety precautions such as work from home policy and social 
distancing. Additionally, we work with 50% capacity, conducting virtual meetings, and avoiding gatherings to limit disruptions 
and protect our employees. 
Diverse Workforce

facilitates inclusion. We view the diversity of our employees and clients in our core markets as a strength, which is why we 
promote diversity and inclusion to create an environment that is optimal for our performance. A diverse workforce brings many 
different perspectives giving us the capacity to be competitive and better equipping us to deal with a dynamic industry. With

opportunities to resourcefully enhance our employees and the Bank’s capabilities. At BdC, we have developed a learning culture

operations and functions, our employees acquire unique skill sets that we continue to develop through our wide range of training

ment's strategy and the requirements and rules of governance was completed. In addition, integrated solutions and modern 
security systems were utilized for all of the Bank facilities and a plan was developed to secure all the Bank’s facilities against the 
dangers of ﬁre per the Egyptian code of conduct. Furthermore, we established our own security company in partnership with
